entry: Southwestern European ethnic group native to the Basque Country, a region around the western end of the [[Pyrenees]] on the coast of the [[Bay of Biscay]]. Basques are characterized by the [[Basque language]], a common culture and shared genetic ancestry with the ancient Vascones and Aquitanians, and are considered among the last remaining direct descendants of [[Neolithic]] European populations. The Basque Country (Basque: *Euskal Herria*) straddles parts of north-central [[Spain]] and southwestern [[France]]. In Basque, people call themselves *euskaldunak*; the neologism *euskotar*, coined in the 19th century, denotes a Basque person whether or not that person speaks the language. Although genetically distinctive in some respects because of isolation, Basques are very typically European in their Y-DNA and mtDNA sequences, which are widespread across the western half of Europe.

Port city in southern [[Iraq]], capital of Basra Governorate, on the Shatt al-Arab near the Iran–Iraq border. The Shatt al-Arab empties into the [[Persian Gulf]]. Basra is consistently one of the hottest cities on the planet, with summer temperatures regularly exceeding 50 °C (122 °F). Founded in 636 as a military camp, it became a hub of knowledge and trade during the [[Islamic Golden Age]]. The Mongols sacked it in 1258, and it came under Portuguese control in 1526 before Ottoman rule. British forces captured it in 1914 during [[World War I]]. Since Iraq's independence it has been an active battlefield, shelled and besieged during the [[Iran–Iraq War]]. Occupied on April 6, 2003, it became the first city captured during the [[Iraq War|invasion of Iraq]]. With abundant oil reserves, Basra has become one of the major industrial cities in the region. Most of its population is Arab Shia Muslim, with a large Sunni minority.

Strait separating [[Tasmania]] from the Australian mainland, specifically the coast of [[Victoria (state)|Victoria]]. It provides the most direct waterway between the [[Great Australian Bight]] and the [[Tasman Sea]], and is the only maritime route into Port Phillip Bay. The strait formed 8,000 years ago, when rising sea levels at the end of the last glacial period flooded the Bassian Plain, a land bridge across which Aboriginal Tasmanians had arrived about 40,000 years earlier. [[Abel Tasman]] possibly detected the strait in 1642 while charting Tasmania's coast. It was named after the English explorer and physician George Bass, who sailed across it with Matthew Flinders while circumnavigating Van Diemen's Land.

Lowest-pitched member of the [[Guitar|guitar]] family, also called the electric bass. It resembles an [[Electric guitar|electric guitar]] but has a longer neck and scale length. Most models have four strings tuned E, A, D and G, an octave below the four lowest strings of a guitar, though five-, six- and other multi-string models exist. The instrument was invented in the mid-1950s to replace the [[Double bass]] in popular music, owing to its lighter weight, smaller size and portability, frets for easier intonation and electromagnetic pickups. Because it is acoustically quiet, it requires external amplification. Fender's Precision Bass, introduced in 1951, was the first mass-produced electric bass.

Short-legged breed of scent hound developed in Great Britain from several now-extinct strains of French basset breeds. It was bred to hunt rabbits and hares on foot, and its ability to ground-scent is second only to the [[Bloodhound]]. The name basset comes from the French word *bas*, meaning low. On average, the breed weighs between 20 and 35 kg (44 and 77 pounds). Its median life span is 10–12 years, and its short stature is due to the genetic condition osteochondrodysplasia.

Double-reed [[Woodwind instrument|woodwind]] instrument in the tenor and bass ranges. It is usually made of wood, composed of six pieces, and is non-transposing. Sound is produced by rolling both lips over the reed and blowing direct air pressure into it. Its range begins at B♭1 and extends upward over three octaves, and its fingering system is complex. Appearing in its modern form in the 19th century, it figures prominently in [[Orchestra|orchestral]], concert band and [[Chamber music|chamber music]] literature, and is occasionally heard in pop, rock and [[Jazz|jazz]] settings. The two modern forms are the Buffet (French) and Heckel (German) systems, which have different fingering systems.

Ancient Egyptian goddess worshipped at Bubastis in Lower Egypt, as early as the Second Dynasty (2890 BCE). Originally depicted as a [[Lion|lioness]], she was later shown increasingly as a [[Cat|cat]]. Bastet and the warrior goddess Sekhmet were eventually characterized as two aspects of the same goddess, with Sekhmet representing the powerful warrior and protector and Bastet the gentler aspect. As protector of Lower Egypt, she was seen as defender of the king and, consequently, of the sun god [[Ra]]. In Greek religion she was known as Ailuros, meaning cat.

Winged mammal of the order Chiroptera, the only mammals capable of true and sustained flight. Bats are more agile in flight than most birds, using long, spread-out digits covered by a thin membrane. The smallest bat, Kitti's hog-nosed bat, has a mass of 2 g, while the largest, the giant golden-crowned flying fox, weighs 1.5 kg (3.3 lb) and has a wingspan of 1.6 m. Bats are the second-largest order of mammals after [[Rodent|rodents]], with at least 1,500 known species, about 20% of all classified mammal species. Traditionally divided into [[Megabat|megabats]] and [[Microbat|microbats]], most bats are insectivores, while others eat fruit or nectar and a few, such as [[Vampire bat|vampire bats]], feed on blood. Bats are important [[Pollination|pollinators]] and seed dispersers, and they control insect populations. As natural reservoirs of pathogens such as [[Rabies]], they can pose risks to humans.

Immersion of the body, wholly or partially, usually in water, for cleansing, relaxation, ritual or therapy. Bathing is most commonly practiced as part of [[Hygiene|personal hygiene]], and is used medically in hydrotherapy and ice baths. Ritual immersion after sexual intercourse or menstruation is required in Islam and Judaism, and immersion forms [[Baptism|baptism]] in [[Christianity]]. Bathing in ancient China may be traced to the [[Shang dynasty]] (1600–1046 BCE), and in [[Ancient Greece]] public baths and showers were established within gymnasiums. [[Ancient Rome|Ancient Rome]] built aqueducts to supply water to its towns, and its public baths, called thermae, had cold, warm and hot baths, rooms for instruction and debate, and libraries.

Room in which people wash their bodies or parts thereof. A full bathroom generally contains a bath or [[Shower|shower]] (or both), a toilet and a [[Sink|sink]], and it may also contain a bidet. Rooms containing only a [[Toilet|toilet]] are called half bathrooms, powder rooms or washrooms in North American English. An en suite bathroom is attached to a bedroom and accessible only from it, while a Jack and Jill bathroom connects two bedrooms. Plumbing must handle large quantities of hot and cold water and the removal of waste, so ceramic, glass and smooth plastic surfaces that are easy to clean are common. Historically, bathing was often a collective activity, as in Japanese sento and Islamic hammams.

Container for holding water in which a person or another animal may bathe. Modern bathtubs are made of thermoformed acrylic, porcelain-enameled steel, cast iron or fiberglass-reinforced polyester, and are usually placed in a [[Bathroom|bathroom]]. Western bathtubs are typically shallow and long, with the bather lying down, while Eastern tubs, called *furo* in Japan, are short and deep, with the bather sitting up. The earliest surviving personal-sized bathtub, a 1.5-meter pedestal tub of hardened pottery, was found on the [[Crete|Isle of Crete]]. The clawfoot style had design origins in the [[Netherlands]] and spread to England, where early bathtubs were made of cast iron, or of tin and copper. Acrylic bathtubs were developed in 1979 by adapting acrylic used for outdoor spas.

[[Superhero]] appearing in American comic books published by [[DC Comics]]. Batman was created by writer Bill Finger and artist Bob Kane, and debuted in the 27th issue of *Detective Comics* on March 30, 1939. In the DC Universe he is the alias of Bruce Wayne, a wealthy playboy and philanthropist in Gotham City. Batman has no superpowers and relies on intellect, fighting skills and wealth, and he vows never to kill any criminal after witnessing his parents' murder as a child. His archenemy is the [[Joker (character)|Joker]]. The 1960s [[Batman (TV series)|television series]] used a camp aesthetic, and the 1986 miniseries *The Dark Knight Returns* by Frank Miller returned the character to darker roots. Batman is the second best-selling comic book series in history, with 460 million copies sold worldwide.

American superhero comedy television series that aired on ABC from January 12, 1966, to March 14, 1968. Created by William Dozier, it starred Adam West as Bruce Wayne and Batman, and Burt Ward as Dick Grayson and Robin. Known for its camp style and upbeat theme music, it ran for 120 episodes in three seasons, the most of any superhero television series until *Smallville* surpassed it in 2007.

Division of cartilaginous fishes, commonly known as rays. Rays are distinguished by flattened bodies, enlarged pectoral fins fused to the head, and gill slits on the ventral surface. With well over 600 species in 26 families, they are the most speciose group of cartilaginous fishes. Batomorphi and the [[Shark|shark]] division Selachii together compose the subclass Elasmobranchii. Most batomorphs live on the sea floor, mainly in coastal waters, though some live in deep water to at least 3,000 meters. Only a few species, such as [[Manta ray|manta rays]], live in the open sea, and manta rays feed on [[Plankton|plankton]]. All skates and some rays lay eggs in leathery cases known as mermaid's purses, while other rays give birth to live young without a placenta.

Capital city of [[Louisiana]] on the eastern bank of the [[Mississippi River]] (pop., 2020: 227,470). Its strategic site on the Istrouma Bluff, the first natural bluff upriver from the Mississippi River Delta, allowed a business quarter safe from seasonal flooding. The city is home to Louisiana State University, the state's largest institution of higher education. The Port of Greater Baton Rouge is the tenth-largest in the U.S. by tonnage shipped and the farthest upstream Mississippi River port capable of handling Panamax ships. Petrochemical industries are central to the economy, with [[ExxonMobil]] among the major employers.

Siege engine designed to break open the masonry walls or wooden gates of [[Fortification|fortifications]]. In its simplest form it was a large, heavy log carried by several people and driven against an obstacle. Later rams were encased in an arrow-proof, fire-resistant canopy on wheels, with the log swung from chains or ropes. Rams were effective because stone and brick were weak in tension and cracked under repeated blows until a breach appeared. An [[Assyria|Assyrian]] ram from the 9th century BC shows defenders trying to set one alight. The introduction of siege [[Cannon|cannons]] in the later [[Middle Ages]] ended the use of traditional rams, although smaller hand-held versions are still used by law enforcement and military personnel to break open locked doors. A capped ram, with an iron or steel head, did more damage than an uncapped one but was heavier to carry.

Criminal offense involving the unlawful intentional infliction of harmful or offensive physical contact with another person without consent. It may be simple or aggravated, and is distinct from [[Assault|assault]], which is the act of creating reasonable fear or apprehension of such contact. Battery is a specific [[Common law|common law]] offense, and under American common law it is any unlawful or unwanted touching of another person. In many jurisdictions it is defined chiefly by statute, and its severity is determined by local law. Canada's Criminal Code does not define battery but provides for assault and assault causing bodily harm. In England and Wales, battery is a common law offense against autonomy, while more violent crimes are statutory offenses under the Offences against the Person Act 1861.

Combat in warfare between opposing military units, and a series of military engagements well defined in duration, area and force commitment. A [[War|war]] usually consists of multiple battles, and an engagement with limited commitment and no decisive result is called a skirmish. The German strategist [[Carl von Clausewitz]] stated that the employment of battles to achieve the object of war was the essence of strategy. A battle ends in victory when one side forces the other to abandon its mission and surrender, routs it or annihilates it; a Pyrrhic victory ultimately favors the defeated party. Until the 19th century most battles lasted part of a day, but [[Trench warfare|trench warfare]] in [[World War I]] lengthened battles to days and weeks. The word is a loanword from Old French bataille, first attested in 1297.

[[Axe|Axe]] designed specifically for combat, with a blade more akin to a cleaver than to a wood axe. Battle axes were designed to cut limbs rather than wood, so their slightly narrow, slicing blades facilitated deep wounds, and their lighter weight made them quick to bring to bear. Axes designed for warfare ranged from just over 0.5 to 3 kg (1 to 7 lb) in weight and from just over 30 cm (1 ft) to upwards of 150 cm (5 ft) in length. Many were used one-handed, while larger examples were two-handed. Scandinavian warriors used them as a stock weapon from the 8th to the 11th century, including the bearded axe, whose trailing lower blade could catch an opponent's shield. Hardwood handles were reinforced with metal bands called langets.

English victory over a larger French army in the [[Hundred Years' War]], fought on 25 October 1415 near Azincourt in northern France. Weakened by disease and the Siege of Harfleur, the English army was blocked on its march to Calais and won an overwhelming victory. The result boosted English morale and began 14 years of English dominance in the war. English and Welsh archers made up nearly 80 percent of the army of [[Henry V of England|Henry V]], and the longbow was used extensively. The battle is the backdrop for [[William Shakespeare|William Shakespeare]]'s play *Henry V*.

Engagement of the [[American Civil War]], fought on September 17, 1862, near Antietam Creek and Sharpsburg, [[Maryland]]. Between the Army of Northern Virginia under [[Robert E. Lee]] and the Army of the Potomac under George B. McClellan, it remains the bloodiest day in American history, with 22,726 dead, wounded or missing on both sides. The battle was somewhat inconclusive tactically, but McClellan turned back Lee's invasion, a strategic Union victory. The result gave [[Abraham Lincoln]] the political confidence to issue the Emancipation Proclamation.

Decisive engagement of the War of the Third Coalition, fought on 2 December 1805 near Austerlitz, now in the [[Czech Republic]]. [[Napoleon]]'s *Grande Armée* defeated a combined Russo-Austrian army led by Tsar [[Alexander I of Russia|Alexander I]], Mikhail Kutuzov and Emperor Francis II. Napoleon feigned weakness, even abandoning the dominant Pratzen Heights, and then attacked the weakened Allied center as the morning mist cleared. The Treaty of Pressburg followed on 26 December, taking Austria out of the war.

One of the last major offensives of the European theater of World War II, also known as the Fall of [[Berlin]]. Marshal [[Georgy Zhukov]]'s 1st Belorussian Front began shelling the city center on 20 April, and the [[Red Army]] gradually took the entire city over the following week against a depleted German garrison under General Helmuth Weidling. [[Adolf Hitler]] killed himself on 30 April, and the garrison surrendered on 2 May. Fighting continued elsewhere until the end of the war in Europe on 8 May.

Military campaign of World War II in which the Royal Air Force defended the [[United Kingdom]] against large-scale attacks by [[Nazi Germany]]'s air force, the Luftwaffe. It was the first major campaign fought entirely by air forces, and its name comes from a speech by [[Winston Churchill]] on 18 June 1940. The British recognize its duration as 10 July to 31 October 1940, overlapping the night raids known as the [[The Blitz|Blitz]]. [[Adolf Hitler]] planned the invasion Operation Sea Lion, which was postponed and then canceled after the Luftwaffe failed to gain air superiority. Germany's failure to destroy Britain's air defenses was its first major defeat in the war.

Engagement of the Second Punic War, fought on 2 August 216 BC near the village of Cannae in [[Apulia]], southeast Italy. [[Hannibal]] and the Carthaginian army surrounded and practically annihilated a larger Roman and Italian army, using the double envelopment tactic. It is regarded as one of the greatest tactical feats in military history and one of the worst defeats in Roman history. About 15,000 Romans survived, most of them from garrisons that had not taken part. Capua and several other Italian city-states then defected to Carthage. The Romans fought on for 14 more years until their victory at the Battle of Zama.
